passages.label: Reading Passage 1
passages.heading: Minds of their own
passages.caption: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1–13, which are based on Reading Passage 1 below.
paras: Virginia Morell explains why animals are smarter than you think. In 1977, Irene Pepperberg, a recent graduate of Harvard University, {{ev:1}}brought a one-year-old African gray parrot named Alex into her laboratory to start teaching him to reproduce the sounds of the English language.{{/ev}} 'I thought if he eventually learned to communicate, I could ask him questions about how he sees the world.'

{{ev:3}}When Pepperberg began her dialog with Alex, many scientists believed animals were incapable of any thought.{{/ev}} They were simply machines, robots programmed to react to stimuli but lacking the ability to think or feel. Although most pet owners would argue otherwise, their claims are highly controversial. Gut instinct is not science and it is all too easy to project human thoughts and feelings onto another creature. How, then, does a scientist prove that an animal is capable of thinking - that it is able to acquire information about the world and act on it?

'That's why I started my studies with Alex,' Pepperberg explained when I interviewed her. They were seated at her desk, on top of his cage - in her laboratory at Brandeis University in Massachusetts. They were clearly a team and because of their work, the notion that animals can think is no longer so fanciful.

{{ev:4}}Certain skills are considered key signs of higher mental abilities: a grasp of grammar and symbols, self-awareness, good memory,{{/ev}} understanding others' motives, imitating others, and being creative. {{ev:5}}Bit by bit, in ingenious experiments, researchers have documented these talents in other species, gradually chipping away at what we thought made human beings distinctive,{{/ev}} while offering a glimpse of where our own abilities came from: sheep can recognize faces; chimpanzees use a variety of tools to probe termite mounds and even use weapons to hunt small mammals; dolphins can imitate human postures and Alex - the parrot - turned out to be a surprisingly good talker.

Thirty years after Alex studies began, Pepperberg and a changing collection of assistants were still giving him English lessons. The humans, along with two younger parrots, also served as Alex's flock, providing the social input all parrots crave. Like any flock, this one - as small as it was - had its share of drama. {{ev:2}}Alex dominated his fellow parrots, acted huffy at times around Pepperberg, and barely tolerated the other humans.{{/ev}}

Pepperberg bought Alex in a Chicago pet store. {{ev:6}}She let someone working in the store pick him out because she didn't want other scientists saying later that she'd deliberately chosen a bird that was especially intelligent for her work.{{/ev}} {{ev:7}}Given that a parrot's brain is the size of a walnut, most researchers thought Pepperberg's interspecies communication study would be futile.{{/ev}} 'Some people actually called me crazy for trying this with Alex,' she said. {{ev:8}}'Scientists thought that chimpanzees were better subjects, although, of course, they can't speak.'{{/ev}}

Under Pepperberg's patient tutelage, {{ev:9}}Alex learned how to use his vocal tract to imitate almost one hundred English words,{{/ev}} including the sounds for a variety of foods. Alex could also count to six and was learning the sounds for seven and eight.

'I'm sure he already knows both numbers,' Pepperberg said. 'But he's still learning to say the words. It takes far longer to teach him certain sounds than I ever imagined but I don't have to make him practice.'

It sounded a bit mad, the idea of a bird having lessons to practice, and willingly doing it. But after listening to and watching Alex, it was difficult to argue with Pepperberg's explanation for his behaviors. She wasn't handing him any treats to get him to say the sounds.

'He has to hear the words over and over before he can correctly imitate them,' Pepperberg said, after pronouncing 'seven' for Alex a dozen times. 'I'm not trying to see if Alex can learn a human language. That's never been the point. {{ev:10}}My plan always was to use his imitative skills to get a better understanding of avian cognition.'{{/ev}}

In other words, because Alex was able to produce a close approximation of the sounds of some English words, Pepperberg could ask him questions about how he understood the world. To show exactly what Alex could do, Pepperberg took him from his cage and carried him to a wooden perch in the middle of the room. {{ev:11}}She then retrieved a green key and a small green cup from a basket.{{/ev}} She held up the two items to Alex.

'What's the same?' she asked.
Without hesitation, Alex's beak opened: 'Color'.
'What's different?' Pepperberg asked.
'Shape,' Alex said.

For the next 20 minutes, Alex ran through his tests. He did some simple arithmetic, such as adding up yellow blocks among a pile of mixed hues. And then, as if to offer final proof of the mind inside his bird's brain, Alex spoke up. {{ev:12}}'Talk clearly!' he commanded, when one of the younger birds Pepperberg was also teaching gave the wrong pronunciation of the word 'green'.{{/ev}}
'Don't try to be smart,' Pepperberg said, shaking her head. 'He gets bored, so he interrupts the others. He's like a teenager; he's moody.'
Many of Alex's cognitive skills, such as his ability to understand the concepts of same and different, are generally ascribed only to higher mammals, particularly primates.

{{ev:13}}'But parrots, like great apes, live a long time in complex societies.{{/ev}} And like primates, these birds must keep track of changing relationships and environments.' They need to be able to distinguish when fruit is ripe or unripe,' Pepperberg noted. 'They also need to categorize things - what is edible, what isn't - and to recognize predators amongst the many species they encounter. And it helps to have a concept of numbers to keep track of your flock. A long-lived bird can't do all of this with instinct; cognition must be involved.'

passages.label: Reading Passage 2
passages.heading: American businesses aim to support employees and their families
passages.caption: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 14–26, which are based on Reading Passage 2 below.
paras: A

Companies of all sizes in the US recognize the importance of family-friendly policies, thanks in large part to the increasing number of people-centered entrepreneurs and company CEOs. {{ev:17}}Many of these go into business themselves as a result of negative experiences they have had in the workplace.{{/ev}} So says Jennifer West, Managing Director of the Ohio-based Business Research Center, a non-profit organization dedicated to studying work-life balance. 'Taking care of employees is a key part of any recruitment and retention strategy,' says West. 'Employers who care about their employees and help them grow take into account the full range of issues and external pressures that employees have and arrange things so that people can manage their lives. These considerations are a conscious part of how people-centered bosses organize their practices and strategies.'
B

One employer who exemplifies this philosophy is Stephen Harper, co-owner and CEO of Plastic Solutions in California. His company manufactures custom plastics, mainly for medical devices, and offers engineering solutions for other plastics needs. Harper believes in having employees who understand the business. {{ev:19}}That's why every two weeks, when his employees receive their salary, they also get an update about the business, including who their new customers are, what successes they've had, and what challenges they are facing.{{/ev}} Harper also includes a 'coaching' section. {{ev:22}}This addresses issues like gossip, which employees sometimes indulge in around the water cooler or the rest rooms,{{/ev}} and which can negatively impact on the morale of staff. {{ev:14}}He encourages people to work their way up in the company, and pays, at least partially, for educational opportunities and textbooks.{{/ev}} {{ev:23}}His employees line up to attend his monthly invitation-only Business Pragmatics seminar,{{/ev}} in which communication and other vital skills are taught, along with ethics and workplace morals and philosophy. {{ev:24}}The structure of his company is very family-friendly, and includes a regular Open House day for employees' families where, among other things, kids can experiment with the company's machines{{/ev}} that manufacture their products and so on. The Harper philosophy pays off. Attrition at the company is low, and many employees remain with the company for much of their career.
C

In Vermont, the Margaret Mills Corporation also strives to be people-centered. It is a third generation, family-run business that sells children's wooden toys internationally, and the company's founder (Margaret Mills) understood all too well the challenges of raising a family while running a business. Like many other like-minded companies, the Margaret Mills Corporation offers liberal leave, flexi-time, good health and retirement packages, and other benefits. {{ev:25}}The corporation also allows workers to have their children dropped off when school is over,{{/ev}} or to spend time with them during the vacations. Annual Christmas and summer parties are standard, and {{ev:26}}this year, to celebrate an especially strong performance, the company took all employees and their families on a 2-day trip to Montreal, Canada.{{/ev}} Says Victor Davies, Human Resources Director, {{ev:20}}'We enable employees to maintain equilibrium between work and home, a policy which ultimately results in a more productive and stable workforce.'{{/ev}} {{ev:16}}It works - this year the company will celebrate six 5-year anniversaries, and one 25-year anniversary among its employees.{{/ev}}
D

For Hazel Gibbs, CEO of Disposal System inc. in Houston, Texas, a waste disposal and environmental cleanup and consultancy firm, the bottom line is keeping her business going. But she realized that it takes a certain kind of mutuality to do that. 'I'm not altruistic,' she says, 'but if everyone understands what it takes to be in business, that's good for all of us.' {{ev:21}}That's why she works hard to ensure that everyone, from managers to workers, realizes that they count.{{/ev}} 'It's not about "us" and "them", we are a team,' Gibbs says. 'When our employees understand what it takes to keep business going, then it works and we can accommodate each other's needs.' Despite the fact that Gibbs sometimes struggles with being taken seriously, she sees this as a long-term challenge. {{ev:18}}'Working mothers still need to be taken more seriously, and so do mothers who are business owners.'{{/ev}} She has two children of her own to think about.
E

{{ev:15}}Family-friendly entrepreneurs are becoming more commonplace internationally,{{/ev}} and they clearly influence those companies which have so far been slow to accommodate employee needs. According to West, it is already possible to document the dwindling workforces of these latter businesses, or the migration of labor to more family-friendly ones. {{ev:15}}What is more, parents are important consumers and investors who can change buying practices.{{/ev}} Further, in the public policy arena, multinational corporations and aid agencies are beginning to recognize the need to integrate social and economic policy and practice. Family-friendly employers are creating a groundswell of awareness that can only result in changing business practices. And as Hazel Gibbs says, when that happens, 'you've got it working.'

passages.label: Reading Passage 3
passages.heading: Literacy and Rural Communities in Australia
passages.caption: You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27–40, which are based on Reading Passage 3 below.
paras: A

{{ev:27}}Little is known about the incidence of literacy in rural areas of Australia, but anecdotal evidence suggests{{/ev}} that lack of literacy skills may present particular problems and have different social costs in rural areas compared to urban areas. Social costs, of course, differ at different life stages. {{ev:36}}For young people, inadequate literacy skills can affect their transition from school to work: for older people lack of literacy skills can reduce their employment options as well as reducing their effectiveness or ability in the workplace.{{/ev}} Assuming life stage differences remain much the same in both city and country areas, it is still possible to make some general comments about differences between urban and rural areas in Australia. {{ev:28}}It is important, however, to remind the reader of the considerable diversity of rural areas.{{/ev}}
B

{{ev:40}}It is not unusual for males in rural areas to have left school early, or to have left with inadequate literacy skills,{{/ev}} and then to move onto farms. This can be due to a number of causes, among which are family pressure or desire to follow the father into the family business, learning difficulties or unhappiness at school, or even {{ev:37}}peer-group pressure from other young males who have decided to work on their family farms.{{/ev}} {{ev:35}}There are numerous areas where literacy skills are required in farming, such as reading directions for (often dangerous) sprays, the mixing of animal feed, the mixing of fuel for machinery, care of machinery, care of animals, and understanding letters from government authorities.{{/ev}} In addition, there are the numerous tasks associated with running a business. {{ev:40}}Although the responsibility for the business side of the farm may be carried by a female partner with more adequate literacy skills,{{/ev}} there remain a number of areas where inadequate literacy skills in males can lead to difficult or dangerous situations.
C

It is difficult to estimate the social costs of low literacy levels for women in non metropolitan areas. Some research in this area has shown that women leave school early and travel to the city to find work: {{ev:30}}{{ev:38}}women's employment options are limited generally, but for women with low literacy skills there is often no alternative to dependence-on family, partner or government benefits.{{/ev}}{{/ev}} Also, according to a 1989 survey, about ten per cent of women living in rural areas were born outside Australia. We can assume that a fair proportion of these have literacy needs.
D

{{ev:33}}{{ev:39}}It is suggested that in times of hardship in farming areas, when there is the threat or actuality of banks foreclosing on mortgages, inadequate literacy skills add to the normal stresses.{{/ev}}{{/ev}} Farmers and others with inadequate literacy skills affected by a rural down-turn have fewer alternatives in employment, less flexibility, perhaps fewer support mechanisms, and therefore more strains both personally and with a partner. It is not inconceivable that the additional stress contributes to marriage breakdown or suicide.
E

Problems can become acute in regional towns or areas which are based on one or two major industries. A proportion of manual and construction workers and trade assistants in such towns have low levels of literacy, but are able to find employment so long as new projects and development continue. {{ev:31}}Shift work and relatively high wages make such work relatively attractive.{{/ev}} Once the development is completed, however, there are few alternative options.
F

In some small communities, there is a tendency for the problem of poor literacy skills to be continued with the next generation, thereby repeating the problem. Economic hardship, the need for children to travel (or be driven) long distances to school, and the low value placed on literacy may mean that helping with farm work is seen as more important than regular attendance at school. {{ev:32}}More children in rural areas than urban areas tend to leave school without completing a full secondary education,{{/ev}} despite increasing school retention rates generally, although there is considerable variation between rural areas.
G

The closeness of some rural communities and country towns sometimes means that people are reluctant to admit their literacy problems. This is generally the case in both city and country locations, cities at least do offer some anonymity for people who make the decision to start a literacy class. In a small country town or rural area, going to a class becomes much more public. {{ev:34}}Tutors in country areas have reported that some students travelled long distances to another town in order to avoid having to reveal their 'problem' in the local area.{{/ev}} Obviously, a change in public perception of literacy problems is needed, if people with low literacy skills in rural areas are to avoid the social stigma which is attached to them in the minds of most people.
